lines.trans: Mom, why did you come here today?
What do you want with that strange teenager?
Max is a serious guy and a good cook.
Why do you always go to extremes?
This is my life, and I decide myself.
First married men, then kids, kids right away.
Stop criticizing me every single day!

words.gram: future, 3rd person singular, perfective; хватит! = enough!

lines.trans: Tell me, did you enroll the guy in school?

words.gloss: to write down; to save (a contact)

lines.trans: I do not want to discuss this now.
Otherwise I could have helped you.
Mom, please, just leave from here.
Alright, I will leave you in peace for now.

words.gram: prepositional singular, masculine; оставить в покое = leave alone

meanings.note: мам! = casual 'Mum!' when calling her
Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'what for'.

examples.trans: Oh, Samson. What have you come for?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Russian perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to come', forming an aspectual pair with 'приходить'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: Security will be here any moment.

examples.text: Не надо, Самсон. Сейчас придёт охрана.
examples.trans: Don't, Samson. Security will be here any second.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'here'.

examples.trans: The white one? Give me the keys.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'today'.

examples.text: Виктор Степанович, сегодня никак не могу.
examples.trans: Viktor Stepanovich, I really can't today.

meanings.note: alone: 'я этого не хочу' = I don't want that

examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'транный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('strange, odd').
Common masculine noun meaning 'teenager' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: What do you want with that strange teenager?

examples.text: Зачем тебе на кухне этот странный шумный тинейджер?
examples.trans: What do you need that strange noisy teenager in the kitchen for?

examples.text: Он ведёт себя на свидании как влюблённый тинейджер.
examples.trans: He acts on a date like a lovesick teenager.

meanings.note: Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'serious' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.
Secondary conversational sense ('important, weighty, influential') (серьёзный человек) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я приехала к очень серьёзному человеку.
examples.trans: I have come to see a very important man.

examples.text: Я приехала к очень серьёзному человеку. Он меня ждёт.
examples.trans: I have come to see a very important man. He is waiting for me.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'boyfriend', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('guy, lad, young man') (informal) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
emphasis: вот поэтому ты и... = that's exactly why you...

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('good, nice').

examples.text: Какое хорошее утро! Лидия Алексеевна, чашку кофе, пожалуйста.
examples.trans: What a lovely morning! Lidia Alekseyevna, a cup of coffee, please.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'cook', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Есть такой английский повар. Я по его передачам научусь готовить.
examples.trans: There is this English chef. I will learn to cook from his shows.

examples.text: Я хочу работать поваром в ресторане.
examples.trans: I want to work as a cook in a restaurant.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'why'.

examples.trans: Why are we going so slowly?

examples.text: Виталик, почему мы так медленно едем? Быстрее!
examples.trans: Vitalik, why are we going so slowly? Faster!

meanings.note: Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'eternal' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.
Secondary conversational sense ('perpetual, constant') (never-ending) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Nothing lasts forever under the moon.

examples.text: Знаешь, что это за часы? Швейцария! Они вечные.
examples.trans: Do you know what kind of watch this is? Switzerland! It'll last forever.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'fall into'.

examples.text: Почему ты вечно впадаешь в крайности?
examples.trans: Why do you always go to extremes?

examples.text: Не надо сразу впадать в панику из-за проверки.
examples.trans: There is no need to immediately fall into a panic over the inspection.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('into, to') (+ accusative (where to)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Abstract feminine noun formed with the Slavic suffix '-ость' ('-ness, -ity') from the corresponding adjective. Common feminine noun meaning 'extreme' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Почему ты вечно впадаешь в крайности?
examples.trans: Why do you always go to extremes?

examples.text: Почему ты вечно впадаешь в такие крайности?
examples.trans: Why do you always go to such extremes?

examples.text: В нашей работе важно сохранять спокойствие без всяких крайностей.
examples.trans: In our work it is important to stay calm without any extremes.

meanings.note: pointing at a thing or a situation; 'это' + noun = 'this is ...'
points at something: это моё = that's mine
Secondary conversational sense ('is') (linking word: главное — это народ) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('my') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
Common feminine noun meaning 'life' in everyday Russian.
меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
High-frequency Russian pronoun ('oneself') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: Я и сама хорошо проведу время.
examples.trans: I'll have a good time on my own.

meanings.en: to decide, to make up one's mind
meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to decide', forming an aspectual pair with 'решить'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: Decide for yourselves what to do.

examples.text: Вот он, телефон! Сами решайте, что делать. Без меня!
examples.trans: Here it is, the phone! Decide for yourselves what to do. Without me!

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('that') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
in 'то, что ...' = 'what, the thing that'
Formed with a diminutive/expressive Slavic suffix adding warmth or small scale. Common masculine noun meaning 'married man' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: То женатики, то дети, сразу дети.
examples.trans: First married men, then kids, kids right away.

examples.text: Подруга всегда советовала ей не встречаться с женатиками.
examples.trans: Her friend always advised her not to date married men.

examples.text: Он оказался типичным женатиком, который скрывал кольцо.
examples.trans: He turned out to be a typical married man who hid his ring.

meanings.note: Derived masculine noun formed with a productive Slavic suffix, used in spoken Russian to mean 'child'.
Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'разу').

examples.trans: You can see it at once.
Now there's a businesswoman, you can see it at once.

meanings.note: impersonal, + genitive: денег не хватило = there wasn't enough money
Secondary conversational sense ('that's enough!') (хватит!) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Gum? I didn't have enough money.

examples.text: Хватит спорить из-за пустяков, давайте лучше спокойно работать!
examples.trans: Enough arguing over trifles, let us just work calmly instead!

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'criticize'.

examples.trans: Stop criticizing me every single day!

examples.text: Хватит критиковать меня каждый день без причины!
examples.trans: Stop criticizing me every day without reason!

examples.text: Легко критиковать чужую еду, когда сам не стоишь у плиты.
examples.trans: It is easy to criticize someone else's food when you are not standing at the stove yourself.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'every', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.text: Аркаш, мне москвичи звонят каждый день. Может, всё-таки передумаем?
examples.trans: Arkasha, the people from Moscow call me every day. Maybe we should reconsider after all?

meanings.note: на днях = in the next few days, or the other day

examples.trans: I'll call in the next few days.
Any day now, on the website.

meanings.note: once; что скажешь? = what do you say?
Secondary conversational sense ('tell me / tell us') (polite request) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Tell us, when will your programme be out?

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('so, and what about') (starting a question: а жвачку?) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

записать.gloss: to write down; to save (a contact)

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'писать'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to write down', forming an aspectual pair with 'записывать'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to save (in a phone)') (записан как... = saved as...) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я знаю, как я у тебя записан.
examples.trans: I know what I'm saved as in your phone.

examples.text: Я знаю, как я у тебя в телефоне записан. Свин.
examples.trans: I know what I'm saved as in your phone. 'Pig'.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'school' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The children are going to school.

examples.text: Привет, молодёжь! Почему вы не в школе?
examples.trans: Hi, kids! Why aren't you at school?

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates

Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to want', forming an aspectual pair with 'захотеть'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: If you don't want to, suit yourself.
They want to build a shopping centre there.

meanings.note: Prefix 'об-' ('around, about') marks encirclement or comprehensive action (stem 'суждать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to discuss', paired with 'обсудить'.

examples.trans: Well, we've been discussing everything here.

examples.text: Ты не обсуждай, ты действуй! Самсонова надо ликвидировать!
examples.trans: Don't discuss, act! Samsonov must be eliminated!

meanings.note: 'сейчас буду' = I'll be right there
Secondary conversational sense ('in a moment') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'can', forming an aspectual pair with 'смочь'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.text: Этого не может быть. Это наша история.
examples.trans: That can't be. It's our history.

meanings.note: with a past-tense verb: я бы подумал = I would think
wishes: купили бы = we could have bought

examples.text: Я бы на твоём месте подумал.
examples.trans: If I were you, I'd think about it.

meanings.note: polite to one person, or to several people
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'мочь'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to help', forming an aspectual pair with 'помогать'.

examples.text: Экскаваторщик — это не мой уровень. Может, поможешь?
examples.trans: Excavator driver isn't my level. Maybe you could help?

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('please') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or discourse tone in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('you're welcome') (answer to thanks) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('here you are') (handing something over) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'just'.
Secondary conversational sense ('easy') (это просто = it's easy) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.en: to leave, to go away (on foot)
meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'ходить'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to leave', forming an aspectual pair with 'уйти'.

examples.text: Уходи отсюда скорее, пока шеф не увидел тебя без формы!
examples.trans: Get out of here quickly before the chef sees you without a uniform!

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'from here'.

examples.text: Я выйду отсюда через две недели. Я решу все ваши проблемы.
examples.trans: I'll be out of here in two weeks. I'll solve all your problems.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('all right') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or discourse tone in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: All right, here you go. There, look.

meanings.note: Russian perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to leave', forming an aspectual pair with 'оставлять'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('to keep, to save') (оставь мне кусок = save me a piece) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I won't leave him on his own.

examples.text: Вика, ну он одинокий. Я же не оставлю его одного.
examples.trans: Vika, come on, he's all alone. I can't just leave him on his own.

meanings.note: оставить кого в покое = to leave someone alone
Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'for now'.
Secondary conversational sense ('while') (as a conjunction: пока я сплю) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('bye, see you') (informal goodbye) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Ладно, ребята, всем пока, увидимся завтра утром на смене!
examples.trans: All right, guys, bye everyone, see you tomorrow morning on shift!
